newsitem.title: USA: Clinton hails drop in welfare rolls.
newsitem.headline: Clinton hails drop in welfare rolls.

text.p: President Bill Clinton took a quick trip to the Midwest on Tuesday to hail progress in reducing welfare rolls and to work for the welfare of the debt-ridden Democratic Party.

Speaking in the sauna-like heat of an old warehouse on a hot August day, Clinton said the welfare caseload has fallen by 1.4 million recipients in the year since he signed a Republican-backed welfare law.
The law ended the federal government's guarantee of federal aid and led to dire predictions about the future of the underprivileged.
"I heard all the reasons that people said it wouldn't work. But a year later I think it's fair to say the debate is over. We know now that welfare reform works," Clinton said.

Since he took office in January 1993, the number of people receiving welfare benefits fell by 24 percent, or 3.4 million recipients, which Clinton called the largest U.S. decline ever in the welfare rolls.

He spoke to more than 500 work trainees, former welfare recipients and local business leaders at the day-long Welfare-to-Work Partnership meeting. They were gathered on the second floor of a warehouse purchased as future worker training facilities by the Mid-Tec Business Consortium of 250 companies.

At the event, Clinton appeared publicly with House Democratic Leader Dick Gephardt of Missouri for the first time since he signed balanced-budget legislation a week ago that Gephardt bitterly opposed.

Gephardt, a possible candidate for the Democratic nomination for president in 2000 that Vice President Al Gore also may seek, was to join Clinton later at a Democratic National Committee luncheon that was to raise $250,000.

Clinton was to speak Tuesday night in Washington at Democratic dinner raising another $300,000. Some of the contributions at both events were large, unregulated "soft money" donations that Clinton has said he wants to ban as part of campaign finance legislation stalled in Congress.

The Democratic Party has reported a debt of more than $14 million as it continues to reel from the controversy over last year's money-raising practices, which are the subject of investigations in both the Senate and the Justice Department.

The new welfare law includes requirements that able-bodied welfare recipients find work within two years and people on welfare have a five-year time limit on receiving benefits. It gave states more control over how to run their welfare programmes.

Opponents had feared the welfare law would throw 1 million children into poverty, deny food stamps to the needy and prompt a "race to the bottom" by states seeking to cut welfare benefits. Experts say a strong economy has helped head off the dire outcome.

Clinton has ordered the federal governent to allocate some jobs for people on welfare and has urged the private sector to do its part as well. He praised 300 St. Louis region companies that have pledged to hire and retrain welfare recipients without displacing current workers.
In spite of the progress on helping get people off welfare, Clinton said there remained much left to be done.
"The most important thing we can do is get the private sector to hire people," he said.

A state-by-state analysis released by the White House on the decline in welfare rolls since 1993 showed wide differences between states. Eleven states saw rolls going down 40 percent or more, led by Wyoming's drop of 68 percent, while California's dropped 1 percent and New York's went down 12 percent. Hawaii's welfare caseloads increased by 36 percent and Alaska's went up 5 percent.
All told, the number of welfare recipients has fallen from 14.1 million in January 1993 to 10.7 million as of last May.
